title: Title, story and genre
short: A heroic epistle (1717) in the manner of Ovid's Heroides: Eloisa, now abbess of the Paraclete, answers a letter of Abelard and relives their love.
body: Peter Abelard (1079-1142), the celebrated Paris philosopher, became the lover of his pupil Heloise (c.1100-1164), niece of the canon Fulbert; after a secret marriage and the birth of a son, Fulbert's men castrated Abelard, who became a monk, while Heloise took the veil. Their Latin letters, beginning after Heloise read Abelard's autobiographical Historia calamitatum, were known to Pope through John Hughes's English version (1713) of a French adaptation. Pope's poem appeared in his Works of 1717. It follows Ovid's Heroides, verse letters from abandoned heroines, and the dramatic monologue of a mind divided between passion and religion. Johnson called it 'one of the most happy productions of human wit'. 'Awful' means awe-inspiring.

title: vestal
short: A Vestal was a virgin priestess of Vesta in Rome sworn to chastity; here, a nun.
body: The Vestal Virgins kept the sacred fire of Vesta and were punished by burial alive if they broke their vows. Pope's classicising word for a nun raises the stakes of the 'tumult' in Eloisa's veins and introduces the poem's governing image of fire and flame (her 'long-forgotten heat', 'the unwilling flame'). Later, 'the blameless Vestal's lot' describes the serene nun whom Eloisa cannot be.

title: Contemplation ... Melancholy
short: Personified Contemplation and Melancholy recall Milton's Il Penseroso, the model for the poem's landscape of cloister, shade and gloom.
body: Milton's Il Penseroso invokes 'divinest Melancholy' and 'the Cherub Contemplation'. Pope's opening transfers that contemplative world to the convent, but makes it a setting for passion rather than peace. Other borrowings from Il Penseroso follow: 'forgot myself to stone' (Milton l. 42), and the 'dim windows' that 'shed a solemn light' (compare Milton's 'dim religious light', l. 160). The compound epithets 'heavenly-pensive' and 'ever-musing' are also Miltonic.

title: idea
short: 'Idea' here means a mental image or likeness of a person, mingled in Eloisa's heart with the image of God.
body: In seventeenth-century usage, after Plato and Locke, an idea is an image held in the mind (OED). Eloisa's heart conceals Abelard's image 'mix'd with God's', the first statement of the poem's central conflict: she cannot separate the human from the divine object of love. The word recurs ('dear ideas', 'each bright idea of the skies', 'adored ideas'), tracing the struggle of images in her mind. The scene of the hand writing the forbidden name while tears try to wash it out dramatises the same division.

title: forgot myself to stone
short: Borrowed from Milton's Il Penseroso, where Melancholy's rapt gaze makes her forget herself to marble.
body: In Il Penseroso (ll. 40-42) the nun-like figure of Melancholy, with eyes fixed on heaven, will 'forget thyself to marble'. Eloisa addresses the walls, rocks and weeping statues of the convent and insists that, though she seems as cold as they, she has not yet turned to stone: the line asserts her living passion against the petrifying discipline of the cloister. 'Shagg'd with horrid thorn' uses horrid in its Latin sense of bristling.

title: Heaven first taught letters for some wretch's aid
short: A praise of letter-writing as a divine gift to lovers, the poem's account of its own genre.
body: Eloisa's apostrophe makes letters a means of transmitting the soul itself, able to 'waft a sigh from Indus to the Pole' (from the far East to the far North). The idea that letters speak for absent lovers and spare the blush is drawn from the Heroides tradition and from the Hughes version of Heloise's letters. The passage also reflects the poem's own situation, since it is a letter answering Abelard's letter to a friend that has fallen into her hands.

anchor: Some emanation of the all-beauteous Mind
title: emanation of the all-beauteous Mind
short: Eloisa first thought Abelard an angelic being, an emanation (outflowing) of the divine Mind in Neoplatonic language.
body: In Neoplatonic philosophy the world proceeds from the One or divine Mind by 'emanation', a flowing out (OED). Eloisa's description of first love uses theological terms: Abelard's eyes 'attempering' (tempering, moderating) each ray shone with 'celestial day', and 'truths divine came mended' from his tongue. The language shows how the love of the teacher was confused from the start with the love of God, which is the source of her later conflict. 'Lambent' means softly radiant.

title: Curse on all laws ... make me mistress
short: Eloisa's argument against marriage, taken from Heloise's own letters: she would rather be Abelard's mistress than the wife of an emperor.
body: In the Historia calamitatum Abelard reports that Heloise argued against marriage, and in her first letter she says she would rather be called his whore than an emperor's empress (the Latin plays on meretrix and imperatrix). The Hughes version renders this as preferring to be Abelard's mistress than lawful wife to the emperor of the world. Pope turns her into a spokeswoman for love as 'liberty' and nature as 'law', a bold libertarian idea that the rest of the poem tests against religion. 'Prove' means experience.

title: Oh, happy state!
short: A vision of love as perfect mutual possession, with no 'craving void' in the breast, which Eloisa once shared with Abelard.
body: The paragraph presents an ideal of equal and reciprocal love ('possessing and possess'd', 'thought meets thought'). Critics note how Pope's balanced couplets give formal shape to the idea of mutuality. The phrase 'craving void' echoes the language of religious longing, preparing the later contrast with the soul filled by God alone. The vision is immediately shattered by the memory of Abelard's mutilation.

title: A naked lover bound and bleeding
short: The attack on Abelard by men hired by Heloise's uncle Fulbert, who castrated him in the night.
body: Abelard describes the assault in the Historia calamitatum: Fulbert's kinsmen bribed his servant, entered his room at night and mutilated him. Eloisa wishes she had been there with her dagger ('poniard'), and protests that the 'crime was common' to both lovers, so the punishment should be shared. Her broken exclamations and the confession that 'shame' and 'rage' choke her speech are typical of the passionate rhetoric of the Ovidian heroine. 'Eloise' is a variant spelling of her name, used here for the metre.

title: victims at yon altar's foot
short: The day both lovers took religious vows is pictured as a sacrifice, with themselves as victims.
body: After the mutilation Abelard became a monk at Saint-Denis and insisted that Heloise take the veil at Argenteuil first, which she did, as the letters report, out of obedience to him rather than vocation. Pope's Eloisa confesses that at the altar her eyes were fixed 'not on the cross ... but you', and that 'love only was my call'. The trembling shrines and paling lamps are the conventions of epic portents, turned to describe a nun's profession. The sacrificial imagery returns at the end with the 'dreadful sacrifice' of the Mass.

title: thy flock ... You raised these hallow'd walls
short: Abelard founded the oratory of the Paraclete and later gave it to Heloise and her nuns; she was its first abbess.
body: Abelard built an oratory near Nogent-sur-Seine and dedicated it to the Paraclete (the Holy Spirit as Comforter); when Heloise's community was expelled from Argenteuil he gave it to them, and the donation was confirmed by the Pope in 1131, as the preface to the Hughes volume records. Eloisa reminds him that the nuns are 'plants of thy hand, and children of thy prayer'. The description of a church built without the wealth of 'dying misers' praises poverty in the spirit of Pope's other satire on ostentation.

title: father, brother, husband, friend ... handmaid, sister, daughter
short: An adaptation of the salutation of Heloise's first letter, which addresses Abelard by every name of kinship.
body: Heloise's first letter opens 'To her master, or rather father, husband, or rather brother; from his handmaid, or rather daughter, wife, or rather sister'. Pope compresses this into two lines, adding 'friend' and closing with 'all those tender names in one--thy love!'. The confusion of sacred and family relations (Abelard is now her spiritual father as abbot) expresses the tangle of human and divine love. The parenthesis 'pious fraud of amorous charity' admits that she prays for him as an excuse to think of him.

title: Black Melancholy ... a browner horror
short: The convent landscape darkens as Melancholy spreads over it, a passage often seen as anticipating the Gothic and Romantic sensibility.
body: Pope first describes the soothing scenery of pines, streams and grots, then shows it transformed by the brooding figure of Melancholy. 'Browner horror' combines 'brown' (dark, dusky, in poetic usage) and 'horror' in the Latin sense of bristling and shuddering awe. The personified emotion transforming the landscape is a technique that Gray, Collins and the later Gothic writers developed; critics such as Tillotson have praised the passage's descriptive power. The 'intermingled graves' prepare for the death-scene.

title: How shall I lose the sin, yet keep the sense
short: Eloisa's casuistry of repentance: she cannot hate the sin without hating the lover, nor repent while she still loves.
body: The paragraph is built on antitheses ('I view my crime, but kindle at the view, / Repent old pleasures, and solicit new'). It reworks the theological problem of true repentance, which requires renouncing the sinful desire, not only the act; Heloise's own letters confess that she cannot repent of pleasures she still remembers with longing. 'Science' means knowledge or skill. The passage shows Pope's mastery of the couplet as an instrument of psychological conflict, and it ends with the prayer that God alone may 'succeed' (replace) Abelard.

anchor: Eternal sunshine of the spotless mind!
title: The blameless Vestal's lot
short: Eloisa imagines the serene life of a true nun, who has forgotten the world and is forgotten by it, a peace she can only envy.
body: The portrait of the 'blameless Vestal' is the poem's image of spiritual calm. Its famous line 'Eternal sunshine of the spotless mind' gave the title to Michel Gondry's film (2004), in which lovers have their memories erased, an apt reading of a passage about the bliss of forgetting. The bride of Christ is prepared for her 'spouse' with a 'bridal ring' and wedding hymns ('hymeneals'), drawing on the long tradition, from the Song of Songs and Revelation 19:7-9, of the soul as the bride of Christ.

title: Obedient slumbers that can wake and weep
short: Pope marks this line as a quotation: it comes from Crashaw's 'Description of a Religious House and Condition of Life (out of Barclay)'.
body: Richard Crashaw's poem, adapted from a Latin poem in John Barclay's romance Argenis, describes the regulated life of a religious community, including sleep that obeys the hour for prayers. Pope's quotation marks acknowledge the borrowing. Pope admired Crashaw and discussed him in a letter of 1710; the debt adds a Catholic devotional voice to the description of monastic peace. The line itself, with its paradox of sleep that is obedient and can weep, compresses the ideal of a life in which even rest is ordered by devotion.

title: Far other dreams
short: At night conscience sleeps and Eloisa dreams of Abelard; the 'phantom' flies when she wakes, and later dreams become wanderings through a desolate landscape.
body: The sequence follows the Ovidian convention of the heroine's erotic dream, but gives it psychological depth: guilt intensifies desire ('glowing guilt exalts the keen delight'), and the oxymoron 'curst, dear horrors' captures her divided feeling. The second dream, with its 'mouldering tower', 'pale ivy' and 'low-brow'd rocks', in which Abelard mounts to the skies and she is left behind, figures their spiritual separation. Such passages made the poem a favourite of later sentimental readers.

title: a long dead calm
short: Abelard, castrated, is pictured in the stillness of a sea before the winds, beyond desire; Eloisa's flames still burn.
body: The simile 'Still as the sea, ere winds were taught to blow, / Or moving spirit bade the waters flow' alludes to the creation, when 'the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters' (Genesis 1:2). Abelard's 'cool suspense from pleasure and from pain' is both the peace of the saint and the coldness of his mutilation; 'The torch of Venus burns not for the dead' is cruelly double. Eloisa's own 'hopeless, lasting flames' are compared to the lamps believed to burn perpetually in ancient tombs, warming an 'unfruitful urn'.

title: Thy image steals between
short: The poem's central line: in every act of worship, the matin lamp, the rosary, the hymn, the incense, Abelard's image intervenes.
body: Each devotional object is invaded by memory: 'With every bead I drop too soft a tear' puns on rosary beads and tears. At the height of the Mass, 'one thought of thee puts all the pomp to flight', and the vision of 'seas of flame' while 'angels tremble round' fuses erotic and religious ecstasy, a mixture that invites comparison with Baroque devotional art and with the verse of Crashaw. In the next paragraph Eloisa dares Abelard to 'oppose thyself to heaven', then reverses herself ('No, fly me, fly me'), a rapid alternation that structures the whole poem.

title: Come, sister, come!
short: A voice from a nun's tomb calls Eloisa to death, where grief and love are at rest and God, not man, absolves.
body: The ghostly summons from 'yonder shrine' is presented with hesitation ('it said, or seem'd to say'), leaving open whether it is supernatural or the projection of a mind in crisis. The dead nun was once 'Love's victim' too, and now a 'sainted maid'. Eloisa's reply, 'I come, I come!', turns towards a death that promises the reconciliation of love and grace.

title: Suck my last breath, and catch my flying soul
short: Eloisa imagines Abelard at her deathbed; the Roman custom of catching the dying person's last breath with a kiss is recalled from Virgil.
body: In Aeneid 4.684-85 Dido's sister Anna wishes to catch with her lips any last breath that may hover over her. Eloisa first desires this intimacy, then corrects herself ('Ah, no!') and pictures Abelard as a priest, presenting the cross to her eyes: 'Teach me at once, and learn of me to die.' The couplet 'O Death all-eloquent! you only prove / What dust we doat on when 'tis man we love' gives a moral to the scene. 'Roseate bowers' and 'celestial palms' are images of paradise and martyrdom.

title: Paraclete; one kind grave
short: Heloise was buried beside Abelard at the Paraclete; Eloisa foresees lovers weeping over their shared tomb.
body: Abelard died in 1142 and his body was brought to the Paraclete; Heloise was buried with him there in 1164. Their remains were moved several times and in 1817 were placed in a tomb at Pere Lachaise in Paris, which became a site of pilgrimage for lovers, fulfilling Eloisa's prophecy. 'Paraclete' (Greek parakletos, advocate, comforter) is the Holy Spirit of John 14:16. The imagined visitors' prayer, 'Oh, may we never love as these have loved!', is ambiguous: a wish to be spared such suffering, or a tribute to love's intensity.

title: some future bard ... feel them most
short: The closing lines imagine a poet, separated from his beloved, who will tell the lovers' story; most readers take this as Pope himself.
body: Pope wrote the poem in 1716, when Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, to whom he was deeply attached, was leaving for Constantinople with her husband the ambassador; Pope's letters to her from this period are warmly devoted, and many readers take the final paragraph as a veiled personal confession. Others stress that the closing is also a conventional Ovidian motif and a claim about sympathy as the source of art. 'Image charms he must behold no more' uses image as a verb, to picture in imagination.
